title: Failed payments on completed orders
description: Return user_id, name, order_id, payment_method, and amount for orders that are marked as 'completed' but have a payment status of either 'failed' or 'chargeback'. Order by amount descending, then order_id ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT u.user_id, u.name, o.order_id, p.payment_method, p.amount
FROM users u
JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
JOIN payments p ON o.order_id = p.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
 AND p.status IN ('failed', 'chargeback')
ORDER BY p.amount DESC, o.order_id ASC
solution_query:
SELECT u.user_id, u.name, o.order_id, p.payment_method, p.amount
FROM users u
JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
JOIN payments p ON o.order_id = p.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
 AND p.status IN ('failed', 'chargeback')
ORDER BY p.amount DESC, o.order_id ASC;
explanation: This query joins users to their orders, then joins those orders to payments so each returned row has both customer and payment context. The two WHERE conditions are important because order status and payment status describe different stages of the transaction lifecycle. Filtering after the joins ensures only completed orders with failed or chargeback payments are returned. The ORDER BY clause makes the output deterministic and highlights the largest problematic payments first.

Filter on both the order status and the payment status.

title: Departments without employees
description: Return department_id, department_name, and region for departments that do not have any employees assigned to them. Order by department_id ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT d.department_id, d.department_name, d.region
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.department_id = e.department_id
WHERE e.employee_id IS NULL
ORDER BY d.department_id ASC
solution_query:
SELECT d.department_id, d.department_name, d.region
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.department_id = e.department_id
WHERE e.employee_id IS NULL
ORDER BY d.department_id ASC;
explanation: A LEFT JOIN keeps every department even when there is no matching employee row. After the join, departments with no employees will have NULL values from the employees table, so filtering on e.employee_id IS NULL isolates exactly those unmatched departments. This is a standard medium-level join pattern because it depends on understanding how NULLs behave after an outer join. ORDER BY department_id keeps the result deterministic.
hints: Keep the full reference list in view, then identify which entries never found a match on the related side.
After the join, look for NULL on a column from the employees table.
complexity_hint: LEFT JOIN anti-pattern: keep rows from the left table that have no match on the right. Can also be written with NOT IN or NOT EXISTS — LEFT JOIN + IS NULL is typically most performant.

alternative_solution.query:
SELECT d.department_id, d.department_name, d.region
FROM departments d
WHERE d.department_id NOT IN (
  SELECT department_id FROM employees
)
ORDER BY d.department_id ASC
alternative_solution.explanation: This alternative uses a NOT IN subquery instead of LEFT JOIN + IS NULL. Both produce identical results here, but NOT IN can silently return no rows if the subquery produces any NULLs — use LEFT JOIN + IS NULL in production for safety.

For each combination, return `acquisition_channel`, `month` (formatted `YYYY-MM` using `strftime`), `total_revenue` (rounded to 2 decimal places), and `order_count`. Include only rows where `total_revenue` exceeds 50 000. Order by `month` ascending, then `total_revenue` descending.
expected_query:
SELECT u.acquisition_channel, strftime(o.order_date, '%Y-%m') AS month,
       ROUND(SUM(o.net_amount),2) AS total_revenue, COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count
FROM users u
JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY u.acquisition_channel, month
HAVING SUM(o.net_amount) > 50000
ORDER BY month ASC, total_revenue DESC
solution_query:
SELECT u.acquisition_channel,

HAVING filters after aggregation — only channel+month combos with > 50 000 revenue appear. ORDER BY month ASC sorts chronologically; secondary total_revenue DESC ranks channels within each month.

title: Top-spender loyalty tier segmentation
description: Compute each user's total spend, order count, and average order value from 'completed' orders. Assign a `loyalty_tier`: `'Platinum'` if total spend > 20 000, `'Gold'` if > 10 000, otherwise `'Silver'`. Return only users whose total spend is at or above the 80th percentile. Columns: `user_id`, `name`, `country`, `total_spend`, `order_count`, `avg_order_value` (both rounded to 2 dp), and `loyalty_tier`. Order by `total_spend` descending.
expected_query:
WITH user_spend AS (
    SELECT u.user_id, u.name, u.country,
           ROUND(SUM(o.net_amount),2) AS total_spend,
           COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count,
           ROUND(AVG(o.net_amount),2) AS avg_order_value
    FROM users u
    JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name, u.country
),
percentile AS (
    SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.80) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total_spend) AS p80
    FROM user_spend
)
SELECT us.user_id, us.name, us.country, us.total_spend, us.order_count, us.avg_order_value,
       CASE WHEN us.total_spend > 20000 THEN 'Platinum'
            WHEN us.total_spend > 10000 THEN 'Gold'
            ELSE 'Silver'
       END AS loyalty_tier
FROM user_spend us
JOIN percentile p ON 1=1
WHERE us.total_spend >= p.p80
ORDER BY us.total_spend DESC
solution_query:
WITH user_spend AS (
    SELECT u.user_id, u.name, u.country,
           ROUND(SUM(o.net_amount), 2) AS total_spend,
           COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count,
           ROUND(AVG(o.net_amount), 2) AS avg_order_value
    FROM users u
    JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name, u.country
),
percentile AS (
    SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.80) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY total_spend) AS p80
    FROM user_spend
)
SELECT us.user_id, us.name, us.country, us.total_spend,
       us.order_count, us.avg_order_value,
       CASE WHEN us.total_spend > 20000 THEN 'Platinum'
            WHEN us.total_spend > 10000 THEN 'Gold'
            ELSE 'Silver'
       END AS loyalty_tier
FROM user_spend us
JOIN percentile p ON 1=1
WHERE us.total_spend >= p.p80
ORDER BY us.total_spend DESC;
explanation: user_spend CTE aggregates per-user metrics. percentile CTE uses PERCENTILE_CONT(0.80) WITHIN GROUP to compute the 80th-percentile threshold. CROSS JOIN with the single-row percentile CTE makes p80 available in WHERE. CASE WHEN evaluates loyalty thresholds in descending order (most exclusive first).
hints: Computing a percentile threshold requires a special ordered-set aggregate function — think about which SQL function handles percentiles.
CROSS JOIN the single-row percentile CTE to make p80 available in the WHERE filter.

title: Normalize event names for display
description:
Event names in the `events` table use snake_case (e.g., `'view_product'`, `'add_to_cart'`). Write a query that returns each distinct `event_name` and a `display_name` version where underscores are replaced by spaces and the result is title-cased so `'add_to_cart'` becomes `'Add To Cart'`. Order by `event_name`.

DuckDB does not ship `INITCAP`, so build the title-case manually by splitting on spaces, capitalising each word's first letter, and re-joining.
expected_query:
SELECT DISTINCT event_name,
       ARRAY_TO_STRING(
         LIST_TRANSFORM(
           STRING_SPLIT(REGEXP_REPLACE(event_name, '_', ' ', 'g'), ' '),
           w -> UPPER(SUBSTR(w, 1, 1)) || LOWER(SUBSTR(w, 2))
         ),
         ' '
       ) AS display_name
FROM events
ORDER BY event_name
hints: The first transformation step is making the string space-separated — think about which operation handles a specific character substitution throughout the whole string, not just the first occurrence.

Title-casing without `INITCAP` (DuckDB does not implement it): split the phrase into words, transform each word so its first letter is uppercased and the rest lowercased, then join with spaces. `STRING_SPLIT`, `LIST_TRANSFORM`, and `ARRAY_TO_STRING` are the DuckDB pieces you need.
explanation: REGEXP_REPLACE(str, '_', ' ', 'g') replaces every underscore globally (the 'g' flag) so the snake_case identifier becomes space-separated words. DuckDB does not ship `INITCAP`, so the title-case step is built manually: `STRING_SPLIT` turns the phrase into a list of words, `LIST_TRANSFORM` rebuilds each word as `UPPER(first letter) || LOWER(rest)`, and `ARRAY_TO_STRING` joins them back with spaces. This pipeline — regex → split → per-word transform → join — is the portable substitute for `INITCAP` in dashboards and reports.

title: List active products per category
description: Write a query that returns each `category_name` and a comma-separated list of active `product_name` values within it, sorted alphabetically within the list. Alias the aggregated list as `product_list`. Only include active products (`is_active = true`). Order the output by `category_name`.
expected_query:
SELECT c.category_name,
       STRING_AGG(p.product_name, ', ' ORDER BY p.product_name) AS product_list
FROM categories c
JOIN products p ON c.category_id = p.category_id
WHERE p.is_active = true
GROUP BY c.category_name
ORDER BY c.category_name
solution_query:
SELECT c.category_name,
       STRING_AGG(p.product_name, ', ' ORDER BY p.product_name) AS product_list
FROM categories c
JOIN products p ON c.category_id = p.category_id
WHERE p.is_active = true
GROUP BY c.category_name
ORDER BY c.category_name;
hints: When you need a single output row per group that gathers multiple values from different rows into one joined string, think about which aggregate function is designed for string collapsing rather than counting or summing.
STRING_AGG accepts an ORDER BY clause inside the function call — ORDER BY inside the aggregate controls the order of the concatenated values, not the output row order.
explanation: STRING_AGG(expr, sep ORDER BY sort_expr) concatenates values within each group in the specified order. The ORDER BY inside the function is evaluated before aggregation and is independent of the query's outer ORDER BY. This is distinct from GROUP_CONCAT (MySQL) which uses a different syntax. ARRAY_AGG is a related function that produces an array instead of a flat string — use ARRAY_AGG when downstream processing needs to index or iterate individual elements.

title: Flag users approaching renewal
description: Write a query that returns `user_id`, `name`, `signup_date`, `renewal_due` (the date exactly 365 days after signup), and `renews_soon` — a boolean that is `true` when `renewal_due` falls within the next 90 days from today. Order by `renewal_due` ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT user_id, name, signup_date,
       signup_date + INTERVAL '365 days' AS renewal_due,
       (signup_date + INTERVAL '365 days') BETWEEN CURRENT_DATE AND CURRENT_DATE + INTERVAL '90 days' AS renews_soon
FROM users
ORDER BY renewal_due
solution_query:
SELECT user_id, name, signup_date,
       signup_date + INTERVAL '365 days' AS renewal_due,
       (signup_date + INTERVAL '365 days')
           BETWEEN CURRENT_DATE AND CURRENT_DATE + INTERVAL '90 days' AS renews_soon
FROM users
ORDER BY renewal_due;
hints: Add an INTERVAL literal to a date column to compute a future date.
BETWEEN works on dates — compare the derived renewal date against a range from today to today plus 90 days.
explanation: DATE + INTERVAL 'N days' adds a fixed duration. Note that INTERVAL '1 year' accounts for leap years while INTERVAL '365 days' always adds exactly 365 calendar days — the difference matters near Feb 29. BETWEEN on dates is inclusive on both ends. This pattern — derived date + windowed flag — is the building block of renewal reminder systems, SLA breach alerts, and subscription lifecycle automation.

title: Convert event timestamps to Pacific time
description: Event timestamps in the `events` table are stored in UTC. Write a query that returns `event_id`, `event_name`, the original `event_time` (UTC), and `event_time_pt` — the timestamp converted to US Pacific time (`America/Los_Angeles`). Return the 20 earliest events by `event_time`.
expected_query:
SELECT event_id, event_name, event_time,
       event_time AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' AT TIME ZONE 'America/Los_Angeles' AS event_time_pt
FROM events
ORDER BY event_time
LIMIT 20
solution_query:
SELECT event_id, event_name, event_time,
       event_time AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' AT TIME ZONE 'America/Los_Angeles' AS event_time_pt
FROM events
ORDER BY event_time
LIMIT 20;
hints: A timestamp stored without timezone context needs to be given a 'home zone' before it can be expressed in another zone — think about how to chain two timezone declarations in a single expression.
Use an IANA timezone name like 'America/Los_Angeles' rather than a fixed offset — it handles daylight saving transitions automatically.
explanation: event_time AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' marks the TIMESTAMP as UTC-aware (TIMESTAMPTZ). The second AT TIME ZONE 'America/Los_Angeles' then converts it to Pacific time. Using IANA names instead of offsets like '-08:00' means the conversion auto-adjusts for daylight saving. This two-step pattern is standard when event data is stored in UTC (as it should be) but business reports require local time. Note: the result type is TIMESTAMPTZ, which may render differently depending on the client session timezone.

title: All user IDs who ordered or raised a ticket
description: Write a query using `UNION` to return a deduplicated list of all `user_id` values that appear in either the `orders` table or the `support_tickets` table. Return `user_id` ordered ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT user_id FROM orders
UNION
SELECT user_id FROM support_tickets
ORDER BY user_id
solution_query:
SELECT user_id FROM orders
UNION
SELECT user_id FROM support_tickets
ORDER BY user_id;
hints: UNION combines two result sets and removes duplicate rows — UNION ALL keeps duplicates.
Both SELECT statements must produce the same number of columns with compatible types.
explanation: UNION merges two result sets and applies DISTINCT across the combined rows. A user who both ordered and raised a ticket appears once. UNION ALL skips deduplication and is faster when duplicates are impossible or wanted. The key interview question is 'when would you choose UNION ALL?' — answer: when you know no duplicates exist, or when you intentionally want to count occurrences across sources. ORDER BY at the end applies to the final merged result.

title: Users who both ordered and raised a ticket
description: Write a query using `INTERSECT` to find `user_id` values that appear in both the `orders` table and the `support_tickets` table. Return `user_id` ordered ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT user_id FROM orders
INTERSECT
SELECT user_id FROM support_tickets
ORDER BY user_id
solution_query:
SELECT user_id FROM orders
INTERSECT
SELECT user_id FROM support_tickets
ORDER BY user_id;
hints: INTERSECT returns only rows present in both result sets — the SQL equivalent of a mathematical set intersection.
The equivalent JOIN would be: SELECT DISTINCT o.user_id FROM orders o JOIN support_tickets t ON o.user_id = t.user_id.
explanation: INTERSECT returns rows that appear in both SELECT results after deduplication. It requires both sides to have the same shape, so it cannot carry additional columns from either table — use a JOIN when you need attributes from both sides. The JOIN equivalent (DISTINCT + INNER JOIN) is more verbose but more flexible. INTERSECT is clearest when you only need the key column(s) and want readable intent-revealing SQL.

title: Users who ordered but never raised a ticket
description: Write a query using `EXCEPT` to find `user_id` values that appear in `orders` but not in `support_tickets`. Return `user_id` ordered ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT user_id FROM orders
EXCEPT
SELECT user_id FROM support_tickets
ORDER BY user_id
solution_query:
SELECT user_id FROM orders
EXCEPT
SELECT user_id FROM support_tickets
ORDER BY user_id;
hints: EXCEPT returns rows from the left result set that have no matching row in the right.
Compare with the LEFT JOIN / IS NULL pattern: SELECT DISTINCT o.user_id FROM orders o LEFT JOIN support_tickets t ON o.user_id = t.user_id WHERE t.user_id IS NULL.
explanation: EXCEPT (MINUS in Oracle) returns the set difference: rows in the first query not present in the second. Unlike NOT IN with a subquery, EXCEPT handles NULLs correctly — NULL rows in the right side do not silently exclude all results. The LEFT JOIN / IS NULL approach is equivalent and more portable; NOT EXISTS is also equivalent and NULL-safe. EXCEPT is the most concise when the shapes match and you only need the key.

title: Revenue subtotals by category and status
description: Write a query using `GROUP BY ROLLUP` to return total revenue (`SUM(oi.line_amount)` rounded to 2 dp) at three levels: per `(category_name, status)` combination, per `category_name` subtotal, and a grand total. Use `COALESCE` to replace the ROLLUP NULL placeholders with `'ALL'`. Return `category_name`, `status`, and `revenue`, ordered by `category_name`, `status`.
expected_query:
SELECT COALESCE(c.category_name, 'ALL') AS category_name,
       COALESCE(o.status, 'ALL') AS status,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.line_amount), 2) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id
GROUP BY ROLLUP(c.category_name, o.status)
ORDER BY category_name, status
solution_query:
SELECT COALESCE(c.category_name, 'ALL') AS category_name,
       COALESCE(o.status, 'ALL') AS status,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.line_amount), 2) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id
GROUP BY ROLLUP(c.category_name, o.status)
ORDER BY category_name, status;
hints: You need subtotals across multiple dimension combinations and a grand total, all in a single result. Which extension to standard aggregation generates multiple grouping levels automatically?
COALESCE(col, 'ALL') replaces the structural NULLs inserted by ROLLUP with a readable label.
explanation: ROLLUP(a, b) is shorthand for three GROUP BY levels: detail (a, b), subtotal per a (a, NULL), and grand total (NULL, NULL). This is more efficient than three separate queries with UNION ALL. The NULLs are positional markers — they mean 'all values of this dimension' — so COALESCE makes them human-readable. The GROUPING() function can distinguish rollup NULLs from real NULLs in the data when needed. ROLLUP is the standard building block for financial summaries and hierarchical reports.

title: Order payment breakdown with FILTER
description: Write a query that returns, for each order `status`, the total order count and three conditional counts: `paid_count`, `pending_count`, and `failed_count` based on `payment_status`. Use the `FILTER(WHERE ...)` clause for the conditional aggregation. Order by `status` ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT status,
       COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
       COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE payment_status = 'paid') AS paid_count,
       COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE payment_status = 'pending') AS pending_count,
       COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE payment_status = 'failed') AS failed_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY status
solution_query:
SELECT status,
       COUNT(*) AS total_orders,
       COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE payment_status = 'paid') AS paid_count,
       COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE payment_status = 'pending') AS pending_count,
       COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE payment_status = 'failed') AS failed_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY status;
hints: A FILTER clause after an aggregate function restricts which rows contribute to that specific aggregate — only matching rows are counted.
FILTER(WHERE condition) is cleaner than COUNT(CASE WHEN condition THEN 1 END) and expresses the same intent.
explanation: FILTER(WHERE condition) is a SQL standard clause (supported in PostgreSQL, DuckDB, SQLite, and newer databases) that restricts the rows fed into that specific aggregate without affecting others in the same SELECT. It is equivalent to COUNT(CASE WHEN payment_status = 'paid' THEN 1 END) but more readable and composable. In databases that don't support FILTER (MySQL pre-8.0.20), CASE WHEN is the fallback. Knowing FILTER signals awareness of modern SQL features in interviews.

title: Monthly order counts with no-gap date spine
description: Write a **recursive CTE** named `month_spine` that generates one row per calendar month from `DATE '2023-01-01'` through `DATE '2025-12-01'`. LEFT JOIN the spine to `orders` on the truncated order month to count orders per month. Return `month_start` and `order_count` (0 for months with no orders). Order by `month_start` ascending.
expected_query:
WITH RECURSIVE month_spine AS (
    SELECT DATE '2023-01-01' AS month_start
    UNION ALL
    SELECT (month_start + INTERVAL '1 month')::DATE
    FROM month_spine
    WHERE month_start < DATE '2025-12-01'
)
SELECT s.month_start,
       COUNT(o.order_date) AS order_count
FROM month_spine s
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date)::DATE = s.month_start
GROUP BY s.month_start
ORDER BY s.month_start
solution_query:
WITH RECURSIVE month_spine AS (
    SELECT DATE '2023-01-01' AS month_start
    UNION ALL
    SELECT (month_start + INTERVAL '1 month')::DATE
    FROM month_spine
    WHERE month_start < DATE '2025-12-01'
)
SELECT s.month_start,
       COUNT(o.order_date) AS order_count
FROM month_spine s
LEFT JOIN orders o
    ON DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date)::DATE = s.month_start
GROUP BY s.month_start
ORDER BY s.month_start;
hints: A recursive CTE builds its result iteratively — start with the seed row for the first month, then define how each subsequent row is derived from the previous one, and include a condition that stops the iteration before it overshoots the end date.
The WHERE clause in the recursive member is the termination condition — when it evaluates to false, recursion stops.
explanation: WITH RECURSIVE declares a recursive CTE. The anchor produces the first row (2023-01-01). The recursive member unions with new rows derived from the previous iteration — adding one month each time. Casting to ::DATE normalizes the INTERVAL result back to DATE. The WHERE month_start < DATE '2025-12-01' prevents infinite recursion by stopping before generating 2026-01. Date spines are critical in analytics: joining fact tables to a complete calendar ensures time-series charts show gaps instead of silently skipping months with no events.

title: Build and parse a composite user key
description: Your data pipeline uses composite identifiers in the format `'country:plan_tier:user_id'` (e.g., `'US:pro:42'`). Using a CTE to first construct this key, write a query that returns `user_id`, `composite_key`, `extracted_country` (SPLIT_PART part 1), `extracted_tier` (part 2), and `extracted_id` (part 3 cast to INTEGER). Order by `user_id` ascending.
expected_query:
WITH keyed AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           country || ':' || plan_tier || ':' || user_id::TEXT AS composite_key
    FROM users
)
SELECT user_id, composite_key,
       SPLIT_PART(composite_key, ':', 1) AS extracted_country,
       SPLIT_PART(composite_key, ':', 2) AS extracted_tier,
       SPLIT_PART(composite_key, ':', 3)::INT AS extracted_id
FROM keyed
ORDER BY user_id
solution_query:
WITH keyed AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           country || ':' || plan_tier || ':' || user_id::TEXT AS composite_key
    FROM users
)
SELECT user_id, composite_key,
       SPLIT_PART(composite_key, ':', 1) AS extracted_country,
       SPLIT_PART(composite_key, ':', 2) AS extracted_tier,
       SPLIT_PART(composite_key, ':', 3)::INT AS extracted_id
FROM keyed
ORDER BY user_id;
hints: Build the composite key in a CTE so you can reference it by alias in the outer SELECT instead of repeating the expression.
SPLIT_PART(string, delimiter, n) returns the nth segment (1-indexed) — parse each position with a separate call.
explanation: SPLIT_PART(string, delimiter, n) extracts the nth segment after splitting on the delimiter. Using a CTE builds the composite key once with `||` concatenation so the outer SELECT can reference it by alias in each SPLIT_PART call, avoiding repetition. Casting the third segment to INT with ::INT validates that the user_id portion is numeric. This build-then-parse pattern is common in pipeline debugging: you construct the key as it would be built upstream, then parse it as a downstream consumer would, to verify both directions are consistent.

title: Category revenue from order line items
description: For completed orders, compute gross revenue by product category. Revenue must come from the individual order line amounts — not from the order-level total, which would be inflated if you join through the items table. Output columns: category_name, category_revenue. Order by category_revenue descending.
expected_query:
SELECT c.category_name, SUM(oi.line_amount) AS category_revenue
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id
JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY c.category_name
ORDER BY category_revenue DESC
solution_query:
SELECT c.category_name,
       SUM(oi.line_amount) AS category_revenue
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id
JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY c.category_name
ORDER BY category_revenue DESC;
explanation: The correct grain for revenue here is the order item: each row in order_items represents one product sold at a specific price and quantity, and line_amount captures that contribution exactly. If you instead join to order_items for filtering but then aggregate o.net_amount, you count each order's revenue once per item row — inflating totals by the average items-per-order (roughly 3×). Anchoring SUM on oi.line_amount keeps the aggregation at the item grain and avoids fan-out entirely.
hints: Use order_items as your revenue source — each row already contains the correct dollar amount for that product in that order.
Join through products and categories to label each line item, but keep order_items as the driving table so the SUM stays at item grain.

title: Distinct buyers per payment method
description: For each payment method, count the number of distinct users who completed at least one 'paid' payment. An order can have multiple payment records (retries, chargebacks) — count each user only once per method regardless of how many payment rows they have. Output columns: payment_method, unique_buyers. Order by unique_buyers descending.
expected_query:
SELECT p.payment_method, COUNT(DISTINCT o.user_id) AS unique_buyers
FROM payments p
JOIN orders o ON p.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE p.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY p.payment_method
ORDER BY unique_buyers DESC
solution_query:
SELECT p.payment_method,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.user_id) AS unique_buyers
FROM payments p
JOIN orders o ON p.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE p.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY p.payment_method
ORDER BY unique_buyers DESC;
explanation: Joining payments to orders produces one row per payment per order. A user who retried payment (failed first, paid second) contributes two rows for the same payment method — COUNT(user_id) would count them twice. COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) collapses all payment rows for the same user in the same method group to one, giving the correct buyer count. The fan-out is real: card has 2,234 payment rows but only 383 distinct buyers.
hints: Think about what happens when a user's first card attempt fails and they retry — two rows appear in payments for the same order.
After the join, each user can appear multiple times per payment method; use COUNT(DISTINCT) to collapse duplicates to one.

title: Brand revenue from completed order lines
description: The merchandising team wants a brand-level performance summary. Write a query that returns `brand`, `total_orders` (distinct orders containing at least one item from that brand), `total_line_revenue` (sum of `line_amount` across all line items for that brand, rounded to 2 dp), and `avg_quantity_per_line` (average `quantity` across line items, rounded to 1 dp). Include only orders with `status = 'completed'`. Order by `total_line_revenue` descending.
expected_query:
SELECT p.brand,
       COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS total_orders,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.line_amount), 2) AS total_line_revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(oi.quantity), 1) AS avg_quantity_per_line
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY p.brand
ORDER BY total_line_revenue DESC
solution_query:
SELECT p.brand,
       COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS total_orders,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.line_amount), 2) AS total_line_revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(oi.quantity), 1) AS avg_quantity_per_line
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY p.brand
ORDER BY total_line_revenue DESC;
explanation: Three-table join links line items to products (for brand) and orders (for status filter). COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) counts unique orders per brand — not line item rows. GROUP BY brand then aggregates revenue and quantity across all line items for that brand among completed orders.
hints: Identify which tables hold each piece of data you need: brand is a product attribute, revenue comes from line items, and the status filter lives on orders.
Use COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) — not COUNT(*) — so multi-item orders are counted once per brand.

title: Acquisition channel purchase funnel

Write a query that returns `acquisition_channel`, `signed_up` (total distinct users from that channel), `placed_order` (distinct users who placed at least one order regardless of status), `completed_order` (distinct users with at least one completed order), `placed_rate_pct` (placed_order / signed_up × 100, rounded to 1 dp), and `completed_rate_pct` (completed_order / signed_up × 100, rounded to 1 dp). Order by `signed_up` descending.
expected_query:
SELECT u.acquisition_channel,
       COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id) AS signed_up,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN o.order_id IS NOT NULL THEN u.user_id END) AS placed_order,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN o.status = 'completed' THEN u.user_id END) AS completed_order,
       ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN o.order_id IS NOT NULL THEN u.user_id END) * 100.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id), 1) AS placed_rate_pct,
       ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN o.status = 'completed' THEN u.user_id END) * 100.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id), 1) AS completed_rate_pct
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
GROUP BY u.acquisition_channel
ORDER BY signed_up DESC
solution_query:
SELECT u.acquisition_channel,
       COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id) AS signed_up,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN o.order_id IS NOT NULL THEN u.user_id END) AS placed_order,

explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves all users (including those with no orders). CASE WHEN inside COUNT(DISTINCT ...) counts users satisfying each funnel condition. title: Support ticket SLA compliance by priority
description: The support operations team tracks SLA compliance: urgent tickets must be resolved within 4 hours, high within 24 hours, medium within 72 hours, and low within 168 hours. Write a query on `support_tickets` that returns `priority`, `total_tickets`, `resolved_count` (status = 'resolved'), `avg_resolution_hours` (average of `resolution_hours` for all tickets in the group, NULL treated as 0, rounded to 1 dp), and `within_sla_count` (resolved tickets whose `resolution_hours` is at or below the SLA threshold for their priority). Order by `priority` ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT priority,
       COUNT(*) AS total_tickets,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'resolved' THEN 1 END) AS resolved_count,
       ROUND(COALESCE(AVG(resolution_hours), 0), 1) AS avg_resolution_hours,
       COUNT(CASE
           WHEN status = 'resolved' AND priority = 'urgent' AND resolution_hours <= 4 THEN 1
           WHEN status = 'resolved' AND priority = 'high' AND resolution_hours <= 24 THEN 1
           WHEN status = 'resolved' AND priority = 'medium' AND resolution_hours <= 72 THEN 1
           WHEN status = 'resolved' AND priority = 'low' AND resolution_hours <= 168 THEN 1
       END) AS within_sla_count
FROM support_tickets
GROUP BY priority
ORDER BY priority
solution_query:
SELECT priority,
       COUNT(*) AS total_tickets,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'resolved' THEN 1 END) AS resolved_count,
       ROUND(COALESCE(AVG(resolution_hours), 0), 1) AS avg_resolution_hours,
       COUNT(CASE
           WHEN status = 'resolved' AND priority = 'urgent' AND resolution_hours <= 4 THEN 1

hints: COALESCE wraps AVG so that groups with no resolution data return 0 instead of NULL.

The within_sla_count CASE must check both status = 'resolved' AND the SLA threshold for each branch — unresolved tickets have NULL resolution_hours and should not count even if they fall within the SLA hours.

title: Users who ordered in both 2024 and 2025

WHERE u.user_id IN (

title: Active brands with above-average product price
description: The product team wants to identify brands whose active product portfolio skews premium. Write a query on `products` that returns `brand`, `product_count` (number of active products), `avg_price` (average price of active products, rounded to 2 dp), and `price_vs_active_avg` (the brand's avg_price minus the overall average price of all active products, rounded to 2 dp).        ROUND(AVG(price) - (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products WHERE is_active = true), 2) AS price_vs_active_avg
FROM products
WHERE is_active = true
GROUP BY brand
HAVING AVG(price) > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products WHERE is_active = true)
ORDER BY avg_price DESC
solution_query:

title: Orders with duplicate paid payment records

title: Session volume and user reach by traffic source

title: Employees earning above their department average

title: Product sales history: first and last sold date

expected_query:

    SELECT oi.product_id,
           MIN(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE)) AS first_sale,
           MAX(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE)) AS last_sale,
           COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS times_sold
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY oi.product_id
)
SELECT p.product_name, p.brand, ps.first_sale, ps.last_sale,
       ps.times_sold,
       (ps.last_sale - ps.first_sale) AS days_on_market
FROM product_sales ps
JOIN products p ON ps.product_id = p.product_id
ORDER BY ps.times_sold DESC
LIMIT 20
solution_query:
WITH product_sales AS (
    SELECT oi.product_id,
           MIN(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE)) AS first_sale,
           MAX(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE)) AS last_sale,
           COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS times_sold
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY oi.product_id
)
SELECT p.product_name, p.brand, ps.first_sale, ps.last_sale,
       ps.times_sold,
       (ps.last_sale - ps.first_sale) AS days_on_market
FROM product_sales ps
JOIN products p ON ps.product_id = p.product_id
ORDER BY ps.times_sold DESC
LIMIT 20;
explanation: The CTE aggregates per-product sales stats using MIN/MAX on the cast DATE. INNER JOIN to products (via the CTE) implicitly excludes unsold products — no sold product can appear in the CTE without a matching product row, but products with no order_items rows won't appear in the CTE at all. DATE subtraction gives the integer day count of market lifetime.
hints: Cast order_date to DATE in the CTE so MIN/MAX return dates, not timestamps.
DATE subtraction (last_sale - first_sale) returns an integer number of days in DuckDB — no special function needed.

title: Registered users who have never placed an order
description: The re-engagement team wants to target users who signed up but have never ordered. Write a query that returns `user_id`, `name`, `email`, `signup_date`, and `acquisition_channel` for all users with no rows in the `orders` table. Order by `signup_date` descending.
expected_query:
SELECT u.user_id, u.name, u.email, u.signup_date, u.acquisition_channel
FROM users u
WHERE u.user_id NOT IN (
    SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM orders
)
ORDER BY u.signup_date DESC
explanation: NOT IN with a subquery is the most direct expression of 'user has no orders'. The subquery returns all user_ids that appear in orders; NOT IN excludes them from the result. An equivalent approach is a LEFT JOIN ... WHERE orders.order_id IS NULL (anti-join pattern) — both are correct. NOT IN is simpler to read but has a subtle NULL hazard: if the subquery returns any NULL, NOT IN returns no rows for the outer query. DISTINCT in the subquery is defensive practice.
hints: NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders) excludes users who have any order — users not in the subquery result are those with no orders.
`NOT IN` returns no rows if the subquery contains any NULL — `NOT EXISTS` is safer when the joined column is nullable.
Add DISTINCT to the subquery to reduce its size — it doesn't change correctness but improves clarity.

title: Duplicate first names by department
description: HR wants to understand naming patterns. Write a query that extracts the first name from `employee_name` (everything before the first space) and returns `department_name`, `first_name`, and `name_count` (number of employees with that first name in the department). Include only department-first_name combinations where `name_count > 1`. Order by `department_name` ascending, then `name_count` descending.
expected_query:
SELECT d.department_name, split_part(e.employee_name, ' ', 1) AS first_name,
       COUNT(*) AS name_count
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
GROUP BY d.department_name, first_name
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY d.department_name, name_count DESC
solution_query:

HAVING COUNT(*) > 1

explanation: split_part(employee_name, ' ', 1) extracts the first token when splitting on a space — the first name. GROUP BY department and first_name creates per-department name buckets. HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 keeps only names shared by multiple employees in the same department. This pattern surfaces naming collisions that might cause ambiguity in directory systems.
hints: split_part(employee_name, ' ', 1) extracts the first name — it splits on space and returns the first token (1-indexed in DuckDB).
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 filters after grouping — it can't go in WHERE because it depends on the aggregate.

title: Support ticket resolution and open rate by country
description: The support operations manager wants a country-level summary. Write a query that returns `country`, `total_tickets`, `resolved` (count where status = 'resolved'), `open` (count where status != 'resolved'), `avg_resolution_hours` (average of `resolution_hours` for resolved tickets only, treating NULL values as 0, rounded to 1 dp), and `open_rate_pct` (open / total × 100, rounded to 1 dp). Order by `open_rate_pct` descending.
expected_query:
SELECT u.country,
       COUNT(t.ticket_id) AS total_tickets,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN t.status = 'resolved' THEN 1 END) AS resolved,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN t.status != 'resolved' THEN 1 END) AS open,
       ROUND(COALESCE(AVG(CASE WHEN t.status = 'resolved' THEN t.resolution_hours END), 0), 1) AS avg_resolution_hours,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(CASE WHEN t.status != 'resolved' THEN 1 END) / COUNT(t.ticket_id), 1) AS open_rate_pct
FROM users u
JOIN support_tickets t ON u.user_id = t.user_id
GROUP BY u.country
ORDER BY open_rate_pct DESC
solution_query:
SELECT u.country,
       COUNT(t.ticket_id) AS total_tickets,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN t.status = 'resolved' THEN 1 END) AS resolved,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN t.status != 'resolved' THEN 1 END) AS open,
       ROUND(COALESCE(AVG(CASE WHEN t.status = 'resolved' THEN t.resolution_hours END), 0), 1) AS avg_resolution_hours,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(CASE WHEN t.status != 'resolved' THEN 1 END) / COUNT(t.ticket_id), 1) AS open_rate_pct
FROM users u
JOIN support_tickets t ON u.user_id = t.user_id
GROUP BY u.country
ORDER BY open_rate_pct DESC;
explanation: COALESCE wraps AVG(CASE WHEN status='resolved' THEN resolution_hours END) to return 0 when a country has only open tickets (AVG of NULL = NULL). The CASE inside AVG scopes the average to resolved tickets only — unresolved tickets with NULL resolution_hours are excluded from the average automatically. open_rate_pct = open / total (all tickets, not resolved ones) measures the fraction still outstanding.
hints: CASE inside AVG limits the average to resolved tickets — open tickets (which have NULL resolution_hours) are excluded by AVG's NULL handling.
If a group could have zero qualifying rows, decide what the average should be (null, zero, or skipped) and reflect that in your aggregate.

title: Users whose Q4 2024 spend exceeded Q3 2024 spend
description: The growth team wants to identify users who increased their spending in Q4 2024 compared to Q3 2024. Write a query that returns `user_id`, `name`, `q3_spend` (completed order net_amount in Jul–Sep 2024, rounded to 2 dp), `q4_spend` (completed order net_amount in Oct–Dec 2024, rounded to 2 dp), and `spend_growth` (q4_spend - q3_spend, rounded to 2 dp). Include only users who had spend in BOTH quarters AND whose q4_spend strictly exceeds q3_spend. Order by `spend_growth` descending. Limit to 20 rows.
expected_query:
WITH quarterly AS (
    SELECT u.user_id, u.name,
           SUM(CASE
               WHEN strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%Y-%m') IN ('2024-07','2024-08','2024-09')
               THEN o.net_amount ELSE 0 END) AS q3_spend,
           SUM(CASE
               WHEN strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%Y-%m') IN ('2024-10','2024-11','2024-12')
               THEN o.net_amount ELSE 0 END) AS q4_spend
    FROM users u
    JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
      AND strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%Y') = '2024'
    GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name
)
SELECT user_id, name,
       ROUND(q3_spend, 2) AS q3_spend,
       ROUND(q4_spend, 2) AS q4_spend,
       ROUND(q4_spend - q3_spend, 2) AS spend_growth
FROM quarterly
WHERE q3_spend > 0 AND q4_spend > q3_spend
ORDER BY spend_growth DESC
LIMIT 20
solution_query:
WITH quarterly AS (
    SELECT u.user_id, u.name,
           SUM(CASE
               WHEN strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%Y-%m') IN ('2024-07','2024-08','2024-09')
               THEN o.net_amount ELSE 0 END) AS q3_spend,
           SUM(CASE
               WHEN strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%Y-%m') IN ('2024-10','2024-11','2024-12')
               THEN o.net_amount ELSE 0 END) AS q4_spend
    FROM users u
    JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
      AND strftime(CAST(o.order_date AS DATE), '%Y') = '2024'
    GROUP BY u.user_id, u.name
)
SELECT user_id, name,
       ROUND(q3_spend, 2) AS q3_spend,
       ROUND(q4_spend, 2) AS q4_spend,
       ROUND(q4_spend - q3_spend, 2) AS spend_growth
FROM quarterly
WHERE q3_spend > 0 AND q4_spend > q3_spend
ORDER BY spend_growth DESC
LIMIT 20;
explanation: CASE WHEN inside SUM pivots the two quarters into columns: Q3 and Q4 amounts. WHERE in the outer query filters to users with nonzero Q3 spend (ensuring 'both quarters' condition) and where Q4 exceeded Q3. Checking q3_spend > 0 is sufficient — if a user had Q4 spend but no Q3 spend, they're excluded by this condition. The alternative of two separate CTEs joined on user_id would also work.
hints: You need quarterly totals side by side per user in a single row — conditional aggregation can pivot a time-period filter into separate output columns.
Filter q3_spend > 0 in the outer WHERE to ensure the user was active in both quarters — users with only Q4 spend would pass q4_spend > q3_spend (comparing non-zero to 0).

title: Sessions with no purchase event by country
description: The product team wants to quantify lost sessions — sessions that never resulted in a purchase event. Write a query that returns `country`, `sessions_no_purchase` (sessions where session_id does NOT appear in events with event_name = 'purchase'), and `users` (distinct users who had such sessions). Order by `sessions_no_purchase` descending.

FROM sessions s
JOIN users u ON s.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE s.session_id NOT IN (
    SELECT DISTINCT session_id FROM events WHERE event_name = 'purchase'
)
GROUP BY u.country
ORDER BY sessions_no_purchase DESC
solution_query:

title: Employee salary distribution by region
description: HR wants to understand compensation spread across regions. Write a query that returns `region`, `band_low` (employees with salary < 60,000), `band_mid` (salary between 60,000 and 80,000 inclusive), `band_high` (salary > 80,000), and `avg_salary` (rounded to 2 dp). Order by `avg_salary` descending.

SELECT d.region,

       COUNT(CASE WHEN e.salary > 80000 THEN 1 END) AS band_high,
       ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 2) AS avg_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
GROUP BY d.region
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC
solution_query:
SELECT d.region,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN e.salary < 60000 THEN 1 END) AS band_low,

title: Payment chargeback rate and amount by method
description: The risk team monitors chargebacks closely. Write a query on `payments` that returns `payment_method`, `total_payments`, `chargebacks` (count where status = 'chargeback'), `chargeback_rate_pct` (chargebacks / total × 100, rounded to 2 dp), and `chargeback_amount` (sum of `amount` for chargeback rows, rounded to 2 dp). Order by `chargeback_rate_pct` descending.
expected_query:
SELECT payment_method,
       COUNT(*) AS total_payments,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'chargeback' THEN 1 END) AS chargebacks,
       ROUND(COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'chargeback' THEN 1 END) * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 2) AS chargeback_rate_pct,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'chargeback' THEN amount ELSE 0 END), 2) AS chargeback_amount
FROM payments
GROUP BY payment_method
ORDER BY chargeback_rate_pct DESC
solution_query:
SELECT payment_method,
       COUNT(*) AS total_payments,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'chargeback' THEN 1 END) AS chargebacks,
       ROUND(COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'chargeback' THEN 1 END) * 100.0 / COUNT(*), 2) AS chargeback_rate_pct,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'chargeback' THEN amount ELSE 0 END), 2) AS chargeback_amount
FROM payments
GROUP BY payment_method
ORDER BY chargeback_rate_pct DESC;

SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN amount ELSE 0 END) avoids NULL — ELSE 0 means non-chargeback rows don't disappear from the sum.

title: Completed order volume and revenue by country and plan tier
description: The commercial team wants a segment heatmap of order volume and revenue. Write a query that returns `country`, `plan_tier`, `total_orders` (distinct completed orders), `active_users` (distinct users who placed at least one completed order), and `revenue` (sum of `net_amount` for completed orders, rounded to 2 dp). Include only country-plan combinations with at least 5 completed orders. Order by `revenue` descending.
expected_query:
SELECT u.country, u.plan_tier,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS total_orders,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.user_id) AS active_users,
       ROUND(SUM(o.net_amount), 2) AS revenue
FROM users u
JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY u.country, u.plan_tier
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) >= 5
ORDER BY revenue DESC
solution_query:
SELECT u.country, u.plan_tier,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS total_orders,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.user_id) AS active_users,
       ROUND(SUM(o.net_amount), 2) AS revenue
FROM users u
JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY u.country, u.plan_tier
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) >= 5
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

hints: The result needs one row for every combination of country and plan tier — both dimensions are part of the aggregation key.
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) >= 5 filters after aggregation, keeping only statistically meaningful segments.

title: Above-average segments with benchmark comparison

Return `country`, `plan_tier`, `total_orders`, `revenue`, and `avg_segment_revenue` (the average revenue across all qualifying segments, rounded to 2 dp). Order by `revenue` descending.
expected_query:

FROM segment_revenue
WHERE revenue > (SELECT AVG(revenue) FROM segment_revenue)
ORDER BY revenue DESC
solution_query:

title: Multi-category buyers by plan tier

title: Users active in Q1 2024 but not Q2 2024

WHERE status = 'completed'

title: Revenue by active vs inactive product status

title: Average support ticket resolution time by priority
description: A support team lead wants to understand if high-priority tickets are resolved faster. For resolved tickets, compute avg_resolution_hours, min_hours, and max_hours (all rounded to 1 decimal) by priority. Order by avg_resolution_hours ascending.

title: Months with refund rate above 10%
description: A finance team wants to flag months with unusually high refund activity. For each calendar month, compute paid_count, refunded_count, and refund_rate_pct (refunded / paid, rounded to 1 decimal). Return only months where refunded payments exceed 10% of paid payments. Order by month.
expected_query:
WITH monthly_payments AS (

    strftime(payment_date, '%Y-%m') AS month,

    SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'refunded' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS refunded_count
  FROM payments
  GROUP BY 1
)

  ROUND(100.0 * refunded_count / NULLIF(paid_count, 0), 1) AS refund_rate_pct
FROM monthly_payments

ORDER BY month
solution_query:
WITH monthly_payments AS (

ORDER BY month
explanation: Counting paid and refunded payments as conditional sums in one pass avoids self-joins. NULLIF prevents a divide-by-zero error in months with zero paid transactions. The WHERE clause in the outer query filters after aggregation — this is the standard CTE + post-filter pattern.

title: Category revenue share per month
description: A merchandising analyst wants to track how each category's share of monthly revenue shifts over time. For each month and category, return month, category_name, revenue, and revenue_share_pct (percentage of that month's total revenue, rounded to 1 decimal). Order by month ASC, revenue_share_pct DESC, category_name ASC.
expected_query:

ORDER BY m.month, revenue_share_pct DESC, m.category_name ASC
explanation: The first CTE aggregates revenue by (month, category). The second CTE sums those category revenues to get each month's total. The outer query joins the two CTEs on month and divides the category revenue by the monthly total to get the share percentage.
hints: Aggregate revenue per (month, category) in a CTE.
Compute each month's total revenue in a second CTE, then join back to the first CTE and divide.

title: Email NULL share — dimension completeness check

Order by user count descending.

title: Monthly completed revenue — date-spine completeness check
description: Before presenting a monthly revenue report for 2023, verify that no month is silently missing from the results. Write a query that produces the complete 12-month date spine for 2023 (one row per month from January through December) and attaches each month's total net revenue from completed orders. Months with no completed orders should appear with NULL rather than being absent. Return `month` and `total_revenue` (rounded to 2 decimal places), ordered by month.
expected_query:
WITH spine AS (
    SELECT CAST(gs AS DATE) AS month
    FROM generate_series(DATE '2023-01-01', DATE '2023-12-01', INTERVAL '1 month') AS t(gs)
),
monthly_revenue AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)::DATE AS month,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS total_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT s.month, mr.total_revenue
FROM spine s
LEFT JOIN monthly_revenue mr ON s.month = mr.month
ORDER BY s.month
solution_query:
WITH spine AS (

    FROM generate_series(DATE '2023-01-01', DATE '2023-12-01', INTERVAL '1 month') AS t(gs)

explanation: The spine CTE generates all 12 month-start dates using DuckDB's generate_series. The revenue CTE aggregates completed orders per calendar month. A LEFT JOIN from spine to revenue ensures all 12 months appear — months with no revenue show NULL rather than being silently absent. This is the canonical pattern for catching missing periods in a time-series report before it reaches stakeholders.
hints: Build the full 12-month reference set first using DuckDB's `generate_series` — this gives you an anchor of 12 dates that drives the output regardless of what the orders data contains.
Combine the date spine with actual revenue data in a way that preserves all 12 months — months with no matching revenue should appear with a NULL total, not disappear.

title: User revenue pipeline — buyer vs non-buyer breakdown
description: A per-user revenue summary is built by combining the `users` and `orders` tables. After the query runs, some users appear with NULL revenue and your team wonders whether those NULLs are expected (users who never ordered) or a data quality problem. Write a validation query that returns three figures as a single row: `active_buyers` (users with at least one completed order), `non_buyers` (users with no completed order), and `total_users` (all users in the users table).
expected_query:
WITH user_order_counts AS (
    SELECT u.user_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS completed_order_count
    FROM users u
    LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id AND o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY u.user_id
)
SELECT
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE completed_order_count > 0) AS active_buyers,
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE completed_order_count = 0) AS non_buyers,
    COUNT(*)                                           AS total_users
FROM user_order_counts
solution_query:
WITH user_order_counts AS (
    SELECT u.user_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS completed_order_count
    FROM users u
    LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id AND o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY u.user_id
)
SELECT
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE completed_order_count > 0) AS active_buyers,
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE completed_order_count = 0) AS non_buyers,
    COUNT(*)                                           AS total_users
FROM user_order_counts;
explanation: The CTE builds a per-user count of completed orders, preserving users with no matching orders. The outer query then uses conditional FILTER clauses to split the count into buyers and non-buyers without a second pass. If active_buyers + non_buyers = total_users, the NULLs in a downstream revenue pipeline are fully explained by users who never purchased — no data quality issue.
hints: Every user belongs to one of two groups — those with at least one completed order and those without. Start by building a per-user completed-order count, making sure users with zero orders are still present.
A per-row conditional inside the aggregate can split groups — `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …)` is the cleanest form in DuckDB; `COUNT(CASE WHEN … END)` is the portable equivalent.

title: Eliminate duplicate events scan — conditional aggregation rewrite
description:
The query below reads the `events` table twice to compute two event-type counts, then stitches the results together with a FULL OUTER JOIN. Rewrite it using conditional aggregation to read `events` exactly once while producing identical results.

```sql
WITH views AS (
    SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS view_count
    FROM events WHERE event_name = 'view_product' GROUP BY user_id
),
carts AS (
    SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS cart_count
    FROM events WHERE event_name = 'add_to_cart' GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT COALESCE(v.user_id, c.user_id) AS user_id,
       COALESCE(v.view_count, 0) AS view_count,
       COALESCE(c.cart_count, 0) AS cart_count
FROM views v
FULL OUTER JOIN carts c USING(user_id)
ORDER BY user_id
```

Return `user_id`, `view_count`, and `cart_count`, ordered by `user_id`.
expected_query:
SELECT user_id,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE event_name = 'view_product') AS view_count,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE event_name = 'add_to_cart')  AS cart_count
FROM events
WHERE event_name IN ('view_product', 'add_to_cart')
GROUP BY user_id
ORDER BY user_id
solution_query:
SELECT user_id,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE event_name = 'view_product') AS view_count,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE event_name = 'add_to_cart')  AS cart_count
FROM events
WHERE event_name IN ('view_product', 'add_to_cart')
GROUP BY user_id
ORDER BY user_id;
explanation: Both event metrics come from the same source table with the same grouping key. A conditional FILTER inside each COUNT computes both values in a single aggregation pass, eliminating the second table scan and the intermediate set operation. For large event tables this halves the I/O and removes the FULL JOIN entirely.
hints: Both metrics come from the same table with the same grouping key — the only difference is which event type each count targets. A single pass over the table can compute both simultaneously.
A conditional expression inside an aggregation can separate subsets of rows without requiring separate queries or intermediate result sets.

title: Pre-aggregate order items before joining to users
description:
The query below joins `users`, `orders`, and `order_items` in a single step before aggregating. `order_items` has many more rows than `orders` — every order row fans out into multiple item rows before the join to `users` is resolved. Rewrite it to pre-aggregate `order_items` to order-level totals first, then join that smaller intermediate set to `users`.

```sql
SELECT u.acquisition_channel,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)       AS order_count,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.line_amount), 2)    AS total_revenue
FROM users u
JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id AND o.status = 'completed'
JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
GROUP BY u.acquisition_channel
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC
```

Return `acquisition_channel`, `order_count`, and `total_revenue` (rounded to 2 decimal places), ordered by `total_revenue` descending.
expected_query:
WITH order_totals AS (
    SELECT o.order_id, o.user_id,
           ROUND(SUM(oi.line_amount), 2) AS order_revenue
    FROM orders o
    JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY o.order_id, o.user_id
)
SELECT u.acquisition_channel,
       COUNT(ot.order_id)         AS order_count,
       SUM(ot.order_revenue)      AS total_revenue
FROM users u
JOIN order_totals ot ON u.user_id = ot.user_id
GROUP BY u.acquisition_channel
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC
solution_query:
WITH order_totals AS (
    SELECT o.order_id, o.user_id,
           ROUND(SUM(oi.line_amount), 2) AS order_revenue
    FROM orders o
    JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY o.order_id, o.user_id
)
SELECT u.acquisition_channel,
       COUNT(ot.order_id)         AS order_count,
       SUM(ot.order_revenue)      AS total_revenue
FROM users u
JOIN order_totals ot ON u.user_id = ot.user_id
GROUP BY u.acquisition_channel
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;
explanation: The original passes every order-item row through the join to users, then deduplicates with COUNT(DISTINCT). Pre-aggregating order_items to one row per order in the CTE reduces the join input from item-level cardinality to order-level cardinality — matching what the final aggregation actually needs. The downstream combination with users then handles one row per order rather than one row per line item.
hints: The original passes every item row through the combination with users before deduplicating — acquisition channel is a user-level attribute, not an item-level one. Computing order totals first reduces what the downstream combination must handle.
After aggregating item rows to one row per order, each order has a single revenue figure that can be matched to a user and summed by channel without deduplication overhead.

title: Replace correlated subquery with pre-computed CTE
description:
The query below uses a correlated subquery to look up each active user's total completed-order revenue. The subquery re-executes once for every user row in the outer query. Rewrite it using a CTE to compute all user revenue totals in a single pass, then bring them alongside the user rows.

```sql
SELECT user_id, name,
       (SELECT SUM(net_amount)
        FROM orders
        WHERE user_id = u.user_id AND status = 'completed') AS total_revenue
FROM users u
WHERE is_active = true
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC NULLS LAST, user_id
```

Return `user_id`, `name`, and `total_revenue` (rounded to 2 decimal places), ordered by `total_revenue` descending (NULLs last), then `user_id` ascending.
expected_query:
WITH user_revenue AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS total_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT u.user_id, u.name, ur.total_revenue
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN user_revenue ur ON u.user_id = ur.user_id
WHERE u.is_active = true
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC NULLS LAST, u.user_id
solution_query:
WITH user_revenue AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS total_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
)

FROM users u
LEFT JOIN user_revenue ur ON u.user_id = ur.user_id
WHERE u.is_active = true
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC NULLS LAST, u.user_id;
explanation: The correlated subquery re-executes the revenue computation for every active user row — O(N) subquery invocations. Moving the aggregation into a CTE executes it exactly once, producing a keyed lookup result. A LEFT JOIN from users to that result retrieves each user's total without repeated computation, and preserves active users who have never ordered as NULL rather than dropping them.

Write a query that returns `signup_month` (formatted `YYYY-MM`), `cohort_size` (total distinct users who signed up that month), `ever_ordered` (distinct users who placed at least one completed order), and `pct_ordered` (ever_ordered / cohort_size × 100, rounded to 1 dp). expected_query:
WITH cohorts AS (

    FROM users
    WHERE STRFTIME('%Y-%m', signup_date) LIKE '2024%'
)

       COUNT(DISTINCT c.user_id) AS cohort_size,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.user_id) AS ever_ordered,
       ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT o.user_id) / COUNT(DISTINCT c.user_id), 1) AS pct_ordered
FROM cohorts c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.user_id = o.user_id AND o.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY c.signup_month

solution_query:

       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN o.order_id IS NOT NULL THEN u.user_id END) AS users_with_order,

             / COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id), 1) AS order_rate_pct,

             / COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id), 1) AS completion_rate_pct
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
GROUP BY u.plan_tier

       COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id) AS total_users,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN o.order_id IS NOT NULL THEN u.user_id END) AS users_with_order,
