GROUP BY u.plan_tier
ORDER BY u.plan_tier;
explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves users with no orders so that total_users is the correct denominator for rate calculations. CASE WHEN inside COUNT(DISTINCT ...) counts users satisfying each funnel stage — using DISTINCT user_id (not order_id) ensures a user with multiple orders is counted once per stage. Both rates share total_users as denominator, making tiers directly comparable regardless of size.
hints: total_users must include every user on that plan tier, even those who never placed a single order. If non-buying users fall out of the result, total_users will collapse to users_with_order and both rates will appear inflated.
Wrap each funnel condition in CASE WHEN inside COUNT(DISTINCT u.user_id) — this counts qualifying users without reducing the denominator.

title: Sessions with duplicate product view events
description: An analytics engineer suspects that the event pipeline is emitting duplicate `view_product` events within some sessions. Write a query that identifies sessions where the number of `view_product` events exceeds the number of distinct products viewed. Return `session_id`, `total_views` (COUNT of all view_product rows in the session), `distinct_products` (COUNT DISTINCT of product_id), and `duplicate_views` (total_views − distinct_products). Exclude rows where product_id is NULL. Order by `duplicate_views` descending, then `session_id` ascending.
expected_query:
SELECT session_id,
       COUNT(*) AS total_views,
       COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) AS distinct_products,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) AS duplicate_views
FROM events
WHERE event_name = 'view_product'
  AND product_id IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY session_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > COUNT(DISTINCT product_id)
ORDER BY duplicate_views DESC, session_id
solution_query:
SELECT session_id,
       COUNT(*) AS total_views,
       COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) AS distinct_products,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) AS duplicate_views
FROM events
WHERE event_name = 'view_product'
  AND product_id IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY session_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > COUNT(DISTINCT product_id)
ORDER BY duplicate_views DESC, session_id;
explanation: COUNT(*) counts every view_product row in the session; COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) counts unique products. If a product appears more than once in the session, COUNT(*) > COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) and the gap is the number of likely duplicate emissions. The HAVING clause is the correct place to filter on aggregated values — WHERE runs before aggregation and cannot reference group-level counts. The NULL guard on product_id prevents rows with no product context from inflating COUNT(*) or masking distinct-product counts.
hints: Within each session, two different ways of tallying view events can tell you whether duplicates exist: one counts every occurrence, the other counts unique products. If the same product appears more than once in a session, the two tallies diverge — the gap is your duplicate signal.
Use HAVING (not WHERE) to filter sessions where COUNT(*) exceeds COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) — WHERE cannot reference aggregated values.

title: 5-stage event funnel by traffic source
description: Marketing wants to understand how sessions convert through the purchase funnel for each traffic source. Using the sessions and events tables, compute per traffic_source: sessions_started (count of distinct session_ids in the sessions table), with_product_view (sessions with at least one 'view_product' event), with_add_to_cart (at least one 'add_to_cart' event), with_start_checkout (at least one 'start_checkout' event), and with_purchased (at least one 'purchase' event). Order by sessions_started descending.
expected_query:
SELECT s.traffic_source,
       COUNT(DISTINCT s.session_id) AS sessions_started,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'view_product' THEN s.session_id END) AS with_product_view,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'add_to_cart' THEN s.session_id END) AS with_add_to_cart,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'start_checkout' THEN s.session_id END) AS with_start_checkout,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'purchase' THEN s.session_id END) AS with_purchased
FROM sessions s
LEFT JOIN events e ON e.session_id = s.session_id
GROUP BY s.traffic_source
ORDER BY sessions_started DESC
solution_query:
SELECT s.traffic_source,
       COUNT(DISTINCT s.session_id) AS sessions_started,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'view_product' THEN s.session_id END) AS with_product_view,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'add_to_cart' THEN s.session_id END) AS with_add_to_cart,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'start_checkout' THEN s.session_id END) AS with_start_checkout,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN e.event_name = 'purchase' THEN s.session_id END) AS with_purchased
FROM sessions s
LEFT JOIN events e ON e.session_id = s.session_id
GROUP BY s.traffic_source
ORDER BY sessions_started DESC;
explanation: LEFT JOIN sessions to events so every session is preserved — including sessions that have no events at a given stage. COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event_name = 'X' THEN session_id END) counts distinct session_ids that had at least one event of that type; sessions without that event contribute NULL, which COUNT ignores. The alternative of four separate EXISTS subqueries is cleaner to read but requires four separate scans of the events table; the single LEFT JOIN with conditional DISTINCT counting is one scan. All sessions in this dataset have at least one 'view_product' event, so with_product_view equals sessions_started — a data characteristic worth noting when presenting the result.
hints: Make sure sessions that never reached a funnel stage still appear in the output — your table combination strategy determines whether they're counted or silently dropped.
COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event_name = 'view_product' THEN session_id END) counts unique session_ids that reached that stage — sessions that never fired the event contribute NULL, which COUNT skips.

title: Monthly order vs payment revenue reconciliation
description: Finance asks: do completed-order net amounts match paid-payment amounts when bucketed by calendar month? For each month, return month (YYYY-MM format), order_revenue (sum of net_amount from orders where status = 'completed', rounded to 2 dp), payment_revenue (sum of amount from payments where status = 'paid', rounded to 2 dp), and discrepancy (order_revenue minus payment_revenue, rounded to 2 dp). Include all months that appear in either table. Order by month ascending.
expected_query:
WITH monthly_orders AS (
    SELECT STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS order_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY 1
),
monthly_payments AS (
    SELECT STRFTIME('%Y-%m', payment_date) AS month,
           ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS payment_revenue
    FROM payments
    WHERE status = 'paid'
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT COALESCE(o.month, p.month) AS month,
       COALESCE(o.order_revenue, 0) AS order_revenue,
       COALESCE(p.payment_revenue, 0) AS payment_revenue,
       ROUND(COALESCE(o.order_revenue, 0) - COALESCE(p.payment_revenue, 0), 2) AS discrepancy
FROM monthly_orders o
FULL OUTER JOIN monthly_payments p ON o.month = p.month
ORDER BY 1
solution_query:
WITH monthly_orders AS (
    SELECT STRFTIME('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS order_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY 1
),
monthly_payments AS (
    SELECT STRFTIME('%Y-%m', payment_date) AS month,
           ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS payment_revenue
    FROM payments
    WHERE status = 'paid'
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT COALESCE(o.month, p.month) AS month,
       COALESCE(o.order_revenue, 0) AS order_revenue,
       COALESCE(p.payment_revenue, 0) AS payment_revenue,
       ROUND(COALESCE(o.order_revenue, 0) - COALESCE(p.payment_revenue, 0), 2) AS discrepancy
FROM monthly_orders o
FULL OUTER JOIN monthly_payments p ON o.month = p.month
ORDER BY 1;
explanation: Pre-aggregating each table to one row per month in separate CTEs avoids any fan-out: orders and payments are on different grains (order_id vs payment_id), so joining them row-by-row before aggregating would inflate both totals. FULL OUTER JOIN is essential because a month might appear in only one table — COALESCE handles the null from the missing side, turning it to 0 so the discrepancy arithmetic still works. Every month in this dataset has both completed orders and paid payments, so no COALESCE-to-0 fires — but the query correctly handles that edge case if the data ever diverges.
hints: Pre-aggregate each revenue source to monthly grain before combining them — combining at the raw transaction level would multiply rows and inflate the totals.
FULL OUTER JOIN preserves months that only exist in one table. Use COALESCE on both sides so discrepancy arithmetic never involves NULL.

title: Support ticket SLA compliance by issue type
description: The support quality team tracks per-issue-type SLA thresholds: technical = 72 hours, billing = 48 hours, account = 48 hours, shipping = 96 hours, product = 72 hours. For each issue_type, return sla_hours (the threshold for that type), total_tickets, resolved_tickets (status = 'resolved'), within_sla (resolved tickets where resolution_hours <= sla_hours), and sla_pct (within_sla / resolved_tickets × 100, rounded to 1 decimal place — NULL if resolved_tickets = 0). Order by sla_pct ascending.
expected_query:
WITH sla_thresholds (issue_type, sla_hours) AS (
    VALUES ('technical', 72), ('billing', 48), ('account', 48),
           ('shipping', 96), ('product', 72)
)
SELECT st.issue_type,
       sl.sla_hours,
       COUNT(*) AS total_tickets,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN st.status = 'resolved' THEN 1 END) AS resolved_tickets,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN st.status = 'resolved' AND st.resolution_hours <= sl.sla_hours THEN 1 END) AS within_sla,
       ROUND(
           100.0 * COUNT(CASE WHEN st.status = 'resolved' AND st.resolution_hours <= sl.sla_hours THEN 1 END)
           / NULLIF(COUNT(CASE WHEN st.status = 'resolved' THEN 1 END), 0),
           1
       ) AS sla_pct
FROM support_tickets st
JOIN sla_thresholds sl ON sl.issue_type = st.issue_type
GROUP BY st.issue_type, sl.sla_hours
ORDER BY sla_pct ASC
solution_query:
WITH sla_thresholds (issue_type, sla_hours) AS (
    VALUES ('technical', 72), ('billing', 48), ('account', 48),
           ('shipping', 96), ('product', 72)
)
SELECT st.issue_type,
       sl.sla_hours,
       COUNT(*) AS total_tickets,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN st.status = 'resolved' THEN 1 END) AS resolved_tickets,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN st.status = 'resolved' AND st.resolution_hours <= sl.sla_hours THEN 1 END) AS within_sla,
       ROUND(
           100.0 * COUNT(CASE WHEN st.status = 'resolved' AND st.resolution_hours <= sl.sla_hours THEN 1 END)
           / NULLIF(COUNT(CASE WHEN st.status = 'resolved' THEN 1 END), 0),
           1
       ) AS sla_pct
FROM support_tickets st
JOIN sla_thresholds sl ON sl.issue_type = st.issue_type
GROUP BY st.issue_type, sl.sla_hours
ORDER BY sla_pct ASC;
explanation: A VALUES CTE defines the per-issue-type thresholds as a lookup table, keeping the SLA logic explicit and maintainable. COUNT(CASE WHEN ...) acts as a conditional counter — no FILTER clause needed and no subquery. NULLIF in the denominator prevents division-by-zero for any issue_type with zero resolved tickets. Ordering by sla_pct ascending surfaces the worst-performing categories first: billing (37.5%) and account (38.5%) are flagged before shipping (75.7%), which is operating well despite its 96-hour SLA.
hints: Each ticket's compliance check requires its issue-type-specific threshold to be present in the same row — bring those thresholds into the query as inline data rather than hardcoding them in a CASE expression.
Use NULLIF(resolved_tickets, 0) in the denominator of sla_pct so issue types with no resolved tickets return NULL rather than a division error.

title: Per-user session count and order revenue: naive join vs correct approach
description: An analyst wrote this query: SELECT s.user_id, COUNT(s.session_id) AS session_count, SUM(o.net_amount) AS order_revenue FROM sessions s LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = s.user_id AND o.status = 'completed' GROUP BY s.user_id. This query is incorrect. Write the correct query that returns, for every user present in the sessions table: user_id, session_count (number of distinct session_ids), completed_order_count (number of distinct completed order_ids), and completed_order_revenue (SUM of net_amount for completed orders, rounded to 2 dp). Users with no completed orders should return 0 for count and revenue. Order by user_id ascending.
expected_query:
WITH session_counts AS (
    SELECT user_id, COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS session_count
    FROM sessions
    GROUP BY user_id
),
order_totals AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS completed_order_count,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS completed_order_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT sc.user_id,
       sc.session_count,
       COALESCE(ot.completed_order_count, 0) AS completed_order_count,
       COALESCE(ot.completed_order_revenue, 0) AS completed_order_revenue
FROM session_counts sc
LEFT JOIN order_totals ot ON ot.user_id = sc.user_id
ORDER BY sc.user_id
solution_query:
WITH session_counts AS (
    SELECT user_id, COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) AS session_count
    FROM sessions
    GROUP BY user_id
),
order_totals AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS completed_order_count,
           ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS completed_order_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT sc.user_id,
       sc.session_count,
       COALESCE(ot.completed_order_count, 0) AS completed_order_count,
       COALESCE(ot.completed_order_revenue, 0) AS completed_order_revenue
FROM session_counts sc
LEFT JOIN order_totals ot ON ot.user_id = sc.user_id
ORDER BY sc.user_id;
explanation: The naive query joins sessions to orders on user_id before aggregating. A user with 15 sessions and 51 completed orders produces 15 × 51 = 765 join rows — so COUNT(session_id) returns 765 (not 15) and SUM(net_amount) returns the true revenue multiplied by 15. The invariant: never aggregate across a join of two fact tables sharing only a foreign key — pre-aggregate each fact table to one row per key first, then join the summaries. The CTE approach materialises session_counts (one row per user_id) and order_totals (one row per user_id) independently, then LEFT JOINs the summaries — summary-to-summary, no fan-out possible.
hints: The naive query joins sessions to orders on user_id before aggregating — a user with N sessions and M orders produces N × M rows, inflating both COUNT and SUM.
Pre-aggregate each fact table to one row per user_id in a CTE before the final JOIN. Summary-to-summary joins can never fan out.

title: Product catalog health: three-anomaly data quality audit
description: The catalog team wants a single summary of known data quality issues across the products table. Write a query that returns exactly three rows — one per anomaly type — with columns anomaly_type (text label) and affected_count (integer): (1) 'inactive_with_completed_orders': products where is_active = 'false' that appear in any completed order placed on or after 2024-01-01; (2) 'category_with_zero_completed_sales': categories that have never appeared in any completed order through any of their products; (3) 'null_launch_date_with_completed_orders': products with a NULL launch_date that appear in any completed order. No ordering required.
expected_query:
WITH inactive_with_orders AS (
    SELECT 'inactive_with_completed_orders' AS anomaly_type,
           COUNT(DISTINCT p.product_id) AS affected_count
    FROM products p
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
    JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
    WHERE p.is_active = 'false'
      AND o.status = 'completed'
      AND CAST(o.order_date AS DATE) >= '2024-01-01'
),
unsold_categories AS (
    SELECT 'category_with_zero_completed_sales' AS anomaly_type,
           COUNT(*) AS affected_count
    FROM categories c
    WHERE NOT EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM products p
        JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
        JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
        WHERE p.category_id = c.category_id AND o.status = 'completed'
    )
),
null_launch AS (
    SELECT 'null_launch_date_with_completed_orders' AS anomaly_type,
           COUNT(DISTINCT p.product_id) AS affected_count
    FROM products p
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
    JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
    WHERE p.launch_date IS NULL AND o.status = 'completed'
)
SELECT anomaly_type, affected_count FROM inactive_with_orders
UNION ALL
SELECT anomaly_type, affected_count FROM unsold_categories
UNION ALL
SELECT anomaly_type, affected_count FROM null_launch
solution_query:
WITH inactive_with_orders AS (
    SELECT 'inactive_with_completed_orders' AS anomaly_type,
           COUNT(DISTINCT p.product_id) AS affected_count
    FROM products p
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
    JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
    WHERE p.is_active = 'false'
      AND o.status = 'completed'
      AND CAST(o.order_date AS DATE) >= '2024-01-01'
),
unsold_categories AS (
    SELECT 'category_with_zero_completed_sales' AS anomaly_type,
           COUNT(*) AS affected_count
    FROM categories c
    WHERE NOT EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM products p
        JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
        JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
        WHERE p.category_id = c.category_id AND o.status = 'completed'
    )
),
null_launch AS (
    SELECT 'null_launch_date_with_completed_orders' AS anomaly_type,
           COUNT(DISTINCT p.product_id) AS affected_count
    FROM products p
    JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
    JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
    WHERE p.launch_date IS NULL AND o.status = 'completed'
)
SELECT anomaly_type, affected_count FROM inactive_with_orders
UNION ALL
SELECT anomaly_type, affected_count FROM unsold_categories
UNION ALL
SELECT anomaly_type, affected_count FROM null_launch;
explanation: Each anomaly is a separate CTE that can be developed and tested in isolation, then combined with UNION ALL. Anomaly (1) uses a JOIN chain through order_items to reach orders, with a date filter and COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) to avoid double-counting products with multiple qualifying orders. Anomaly (2) uses NOT EXISTS with a correlated subquery that traces categories through products → order_items → orders — the anti-join pattern for 'category with no qualifying rows.' Anomaly (3) is a NULL check combined with the same join chain. UNION ALL (not UNION) is correct here: the three anomaly types are mutually distinct by construction, so deduplication is unnecessary and UNION ALL is cheaper.
hints: Compute each anomaly's affected count independently, then stack the three results into a single output — three separate subproblems that share no data and each produce one row.
The 'zero completed sales' anomaly is an anti-join: NOT EXISTS tracing categories through their products to completed orders is cleaner than a LEFT JOIN / IS NULL.
